mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes E Class 550 engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supply-only rebuilt M273 and M278 engines range from £4,000 to £8,500 depending on engine code and condition. With specialist fitting, budget £4,500-£9,500 total. M113.967 (E 500, 306 hp, 2002-2006): rebuilt £3,200-£5,000. M273 (E 500 / E 550, 388 hp, 2006-2011): rebuilt £4,000-£6,500. M278 (E 550, 408 hp twin-turbo, 2011-2016): rebuilt £5,500-£8,500. Labour adds £500-£1,000 depending on specialist location.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of timing chain failure in an E Class 500 / 550?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cold-start rattling that disappears after a few seconds is the classic early warning sign. On the M278, a service bulletin was issued for chain tensioner issues. Rattling on cold start, particularly from the front of the engine. Metallic clanging sounds from the timing chain area. Check engine light with cam-correlation fault codes. Timing chain replacement at a specialist costs £1,500-£2,800.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine on an older E Class 500 or 550?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the car is otherwise sound. W211 E 500 examples command £3,000-£7,000 used, while W212 E 550 examples command £6,000-£15,000, making replacement viable. A quality rebuilt M113 costs £3,200-£5,000 supply only. A quality rebuilt M273 costs £4,000-£6,500 supply only. A quality rebuilt M278 costs £5,500-£8,500 supply only. V8-engined E-Classes are increasingly sought after as modern classics. A replacement engine with warranty costs less than financing a newer car.

mainEntity.name: What causes the M273 balance shaft idler gear to fail on E 500 / 550 models?

acceptedAnswer.text: The idler gear in the M273's timing drive system can wear prematurely, causing timing faults and misfire codes. This was addressed on later production engines. Idler gear wear typically occurs between 60,000-100,000 miles. Check engine light with timing correlation codes is the main symptom. Early M273 engines (up to serial 27396230 088611) are most susceptible. Idler gear and timing chain replacement at a specialist costs £1,500-£2,800.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the M113, M273 and M278 engines in the E Class?

acceptedAnswer.text: The M113 is a 5.0-litre naturally aspirated SOHC V8 (306 hp). The M273 is a 5.5-litre naturally aspirated DOHC V8 (388 hp). The M278 is a 4.7-litre twin-turbo DOHC V8 (408 hp). M113: 5.0L, SOHC, 3 valves/cylinder, 306 hp, 460 Nm - robust but dated. M273: 5.5L, DOHC, 4 valves/cylinder, 388 hp, 530 Nm - more powerful but has idler gear issues. M278: 4.7L twin-turbo, DOHC, 4 valves/cylinder, 408 hp, 600 Nm - most powerful but complex. The M278 replaced the M273 in 2011 and is based on the S-Class M278 engine.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes E Class 550 engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With proper maintenance and regular oil changes, M113, M273 and M278 engines regularly reach 150,000-200,000+ miles. The M113 is considered the most durable of the three. M113 V8 bottom ends are exceptionally robust when properly maintained. Timing chain inspection at 80k-100k miles is recommended across all three. The M278's turbochargers add complexity but are generally reliable. Regular oil changes (8,000 miles) are critical for timing chain and turbo life.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz E Class 500 / 550 - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The E 500 and E 550 badges represented Mercedes-Benz's flagship V8 petrol offerings across the W211 and W212 E-Class generations. The E 500 launched with the M113 5.0-litre V8 - a robust three-valve SOHC design - before being replaced by the more powerful M273 5.5-litre V8 in 2006. The E 550 badge arrived with the W212 generation, initially powered by the M273 5.5-litre V8 before transitioning to the M278 4.7-litre twin-turbo V8 in 2011 - a modern, more efficient powerplant that would define the E-Class V8 experience until the model's discontinuation. These V8-engined E-Classes represent the pinnacle of non-AMG E-Class performance, offering effortless power and refinement.

milestones.description: **2002** - W211 E 500 launched with M113.967 5.0-litre V8, 225 kW (306 hp), 460 Nm
**2006** - W211 facelift E 500 gains M273 5.5-litre V8, 285 kW (388 hp), 530 Nm
**2009** - W212 generation launched; E 500 badge replaced by E 550 in UK market
**2011** - M278 4.7-litre twin-turbo V8 introduced, replacing M273 in E 550
**2016** - W212 production ends; V8-engined E-Class models discontinued in favour of AMG-only V8 offerings

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes E Class 500 / 550 Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The V8-engined E Class 500 and 550 represent the pinnacle of non-AMG E-Class performance. The M113 is a robust, proven design, while the M273 and M278 bring more power but also more complexity. Timing chain issues affect all three engine families to varying degrees, while the M273's balance shaft idler gear and the M278's oil seepage into wiring harnesses are well-documented weaknesses. Every rebuilt engine supplied through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components designed to address the original failure point, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited mileage warranty. Below, we break down what these failures cost to fix and when replacement is the smarter option.

problems.h4: Timing Chain & Tensioner Wear - The V8 Achilles Heel Across All Generations
problems.rootCause: Timing chain tensioners and guides wear over time, particularly when oil change intervals are extended. The M113 is known for chain stretch at around 100,000 miles. On the M278, a service bulletin (LI05.10-P-056435) was issued for chain tensioner issues. Cold-start rattling - often described as "marbles in a can" - is the classic early warning sign. If ignored, the chain can jump a tooth, risking bent valves and catastrophic engine failure.

repairOptions.longevity: 80,000-100,000 miles; effective if rattle is minimal

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of timing chain(s), tensioner(s), guides and sprockets
repairOptions.longevity: When chain has stretched or rattle persists

repairOptions.longevity: When chain has jumped causing valvetrain damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical W211 E 500 is worth £3,000-£7,000 depending on condition and mileage; a W212 E 550 commands £6,000-£15,000【INDUSTRY ESTIMATE】. If the vehicle is worth under £4,000, a used engine or timing chain repair is usually the pragmatic choice. For W212 cars worth £8,000+, a rebuilt engine with warranty can be justified if the rest of the car is sound.
problems.recommendation: The cold-start rattle is your early warning - don't ignore it. A specialist timing chain replacement at £1,500-£2,800 is significantly cheaper than the £4,000+ engine replacement if the chain jumps. On the M278, check if the timing chain tensioner service bulletin has been applied - this is a known issue that Mercedes addressed through warranty campaigns. On the M113, regular oil changes (8,000 miles) are critical for timing chain life.

problems.h4: M113 & M273 Oil Leaks - Valve Cover Gaskets and Cam Seals
problems.rootCause: Valve cover gaskets and cam seals degrade over time, allowing oil to leak onto the exhaust manifold. This is a very common issue on the M113. On the M273, camshaft cover seals can fail. The burning oil smell and smoke from the engine bay are the classic warning signs.

problems.recommendation: Oil leaks are a fact of life on higher-mileage M113 and M273 engines. If you notice a burning oil smell or smoke from the engine bay, have the valve cover gaskets inspected promptly. problems.h4: M273 Balance Shaft Idler Gear Wear - The V8 Timing Weakness
problems.rootCause: The M273 V8 uses an idler gear in the timing drive system. This gear can wear prematurely, causing timing faults and misfire codes. The issue is similar to the M272 balance shaft problem and was addressed on later production engines. Early M273 engines (up to serial number 27396230 088611) are most susceptible. Symptoms include check engine lights with timing correlation codes and engine misfires.

problems.recommendation: The M273 idler gear issue is a known design weakness on early engines. If you own a 2006-2008 E 500 or E 550, check the engine serial number against the known affected range. problems.group: M278 Oil Seepage into Wiring Harness
problems.h4: M278 Oil Seepage into Wiring Harness - The Twin-Turbo ECU Threat
problems.rootCause: The M278 is known for oil seepage from camshaft position sensors and camshaft solenoid adjuster magnets. This oil can travel through the wiring harness to the ECU, causing misfires, rough running, and potentially ECU failure. The M278 is otherwise a reliable engine, but this issue requires prompt attention. Coolant loss and cylinder scoring have also been reported.

ECU replacement at £1,500-£3,000 is still far cheaper than a £5,500+ engine replacement.
problems.recommendation: The M278's oil seepage issue is well-documented - if you experience misfires, rough running, or a check engine light on your E 550, have the camshaft sensors and wiring harness inspected promptly. Early detection can prevent ECU damage. Regular maintenance and using high-quality oil are essential for M278 longevity. If oil has already reached the ECU, replacement is the only safe option - but the £1,500-£3,000 cost is still far less than an engine replacement.
